claim: Quantitative RT-PCR confirmed substantial steady-state levels of Ptprg mRNA in basilar arteries.

claim: Acetylcholine-induced vasorelaxation of basilar arteries from RPTPγ KO mice was suppressed in presence of CO2/HCO3– mostly because of attenuated NO-dependent signaling.

evidence: Based on myography experiments with L-NAME shown in Figure 2D-G.

claim: The diminished vasorelaxation of basilar arteries in response to SLIGRL-amide was mostly explained by smaller endothelium-dependent hyperpolarization (EDH)-type responses.
source: In contrast, the diminished vasorelaxation of basilar arteries in response to SLIGRL-amide (Figure 3D–F) and of mesenteric and coronary arteries in response to acetylcholine (Figure 2J–L and Figure 2N–P) and SLIGRL-amide (Figure 3J,K,M,N) was mostly explained by smaller endothelium-dependent hyperpolarization (EDH)-type responses that were L-NAME-insensitive but inhibited by apamin and TRAM-34.
evidence: Based on myography experiments with L-NAME, apamin, and TRAM-34 shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: In nominally CO2/HCO3–-free, HEPES-buffered solutions, there was no RPTPγ-dependent difference in overall vasorelaxant function of basilar arteries in response to acetylcholine.
source: In order to evaluate whether RPTPγ-dependent signaling is influenced by HCO3– in the vascular wall, we next repeated studies of endothelium-dependent vasorelaxation using nominally CO2/HCO3–-free, HEPES-buffered solutions (Figure 4). Under these conditions, we saw no RPTPγ-dependent differences in overall vasorelaxant function of basilar or mesenteric arteries in response to acetylcholine (Figure 4A,B,G) or SLIGRL-amide (Figure 4K,L,P).
evidence: Based on myography experiments in CO2/HCO3–-free solutions shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Expression of endothelial NO-synthase (eNOS) is equal between basilar arteries from RPTPγ KO and WT mice.
source: We first evaluated whether the difference in vasorelaxation between arteries from RPTPγ KO and WT mice depends on a change in expression of the endothelial NO-synthase (eNOS). Based on immunoblotting of basilar (Figure 5A) and mesenteric (Figure 5D) arteries, we found equal eNOS expression between arteries from RPTPγ KO and WT mice.
evidence: Based on immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of endothelial NO-synthase (eNOS) is equal between mesenteric arteries from RPTPγ KO and WT mice.

claim: Spermine NONOate produced equivalent vasorelaxation in basilar arteries from RPTPγ KO and WT mice in presence of CO2/HCO3–.
source: We also evaluated whether the smooth muscle vasorelaxant responses to exogenous NO differ between arteries from WT and RPTPγ KO mice. In presence of CO2/HCO3–, spermine NONOate and S-nitroso-N-acetylpenicillamine (SNAP) produced equivalent vasorelaxation in basilar and mesenteric arteries from RPTPγ KO and WT mice (Figure 5B,C,E,F).
evidence: Based on myography experiments with NO donors shown in Figure 5B.

evidence: Based on Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 5H,J.

claim: In the nominal absence of CO2/HCO3–, there was no significant difference between the intracellular Ca2+ responses of endothelial cells in basilar arteries from WT and RPTPγ KO mice.

claim: Intracellular pH of endothelial cells in basilar arteries was similar for RPTPγ KO and WT mice, irrespective of whether experiments were performed with or without CO2/HCO3–.
source: Therefore, we next evaluated whether RPTPγ KO influences intracellular pH—measured using the pH-sensitive fluorophore BCECF—in endothelial cells of small arteries. In basilar (Figure 5P) as well as mesenteric (Figure 5Q) arteries, intracellular pH of the endothelial cells was similar for RPTPγ KO and WT mice, irrespective of whether experiments were performed with or without CO2/HCO3–.
evidence: Based on intracellular pH measurements shown in Figure 5P.

claim: Intracellular pH of endothelial cells in mesenteric arteries was similar for RPTPγ KO and WT mice, irrespective of whether experiments were performed with or without CO2/HCO3–.

claim: Omission of CO2/HCO3– from the bath solutions had no net effect on endothelial steady-state intracellular pH.
source: Omission of CO2/HCO3– from the bath solutions had no net effect on endothelial steady-state intracellular pH (Figure 5P,Q), which is consistent with previous studies based on arteries from C57BL/6 mice (Boedtkjer et al., 2011; Boedtkjer et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on intracellular pH measurements shown in Figure 5P,Q and consistent with previous studies (Boedtkjer et al., 2011; Boedtkjer et al., 2012).

claim: There was no difference in resting blood pressure between RPTPγ KO and WT mice.

evidence: Based on radiotelemetry measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There was no difference in resting heart rate between RPTPγ KO and WT mice.

evidence: Based on radiotelemetry measurements during L-NAME treatment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When mice were ventilated to a normal expiratory end-tidal CO2 fraction (FETCO2) of 3.5%, arterial blood gas parameters were very similar in RPTPγ KO and WT mice.
source: When mice were ventilated to a normal expiratory end-tidal CO2 fraction (FETCO2) of 3.5%, arterial blood gas parameters were very similar in RPTPγ KO and WT mice (Table 1) consistent with previous findings (Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on arterial blood gas measurements shown in Table 1 and consistent with previous findings (Zhou et al., 2016).

claim: Hyperventilating mice until FETCO2 was lowered to 2% caused a decrease in PaCO2.
source: Hyperventilating mice until FETCO2 was lowered to 2% caused the expected decrease in PaCO2 and increase in pHa (Table 1).
evidence: Based on arterial blood gas measurements during hyperventilation shown in Table 1.

claim: Hyperventilating mice until FETCO2 was lowered to 2% caused an increase in pHa.
source: Hyperventilating mice until FETCO2 was lowered to 2% caused the expected decrease in PaCO2 and increase in pHa (Table 1).
evidence: Based on arterial blood gas measurements during hyperventilation shown in Table 1.

claim: The mean arterial blood pressure of WT mice increased around 20% during hyperventilation.
source: The mean arterial blood pressure of WT mice increased around 20% during hyperventilation and this blood pressure response was reduced by approximately 1/3 in RPTPγ KO mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on blood pressure measurements during hyperventilation shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The hyperventilation-induced blood pressure response was reduced by approximately 1/3 in RPTPγ KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: The mean arterial blood pressure of WT mice increased around 20% during hyperventilation and this blood pressure response was reduced by approximately 1/3 in RPTPγ KO mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on blood pressure measurements during hyperventilation shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Tissue perfusion in the somatosensory barrel cortex increased twice as much in RPTPγ KO mice compared to WT mice during whisker stimulation.
source: Tissue perfusion in the somatosensory barrel cortex increased twice as much in RPTPγ KO mice compared to WT mice during whisker stimulation (Figure 6E).
evidence: Based on laser speckle imaging during whisker stimulation shown in Figure 6E.

claim: During hyperventilation, cerebral perfusion showed a 30% smaller drop in RPTPγ KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: Under these conditions, cerebral vasoconstriction is expected in WT mice based on the combined effect of alkalosis and decreased [HCO3–] (Boedtkjer et al., 2016c). If RPTPγ is required for sensing of HCO3–, only the effect of the elevated pH is expected in the RPTPγ KO mice; and indeed, we saw a 30% smaller drop in cerebral perfusion in RPTPγ KO mice compared to WT mice during hyperventilation (Figure 6F).
evidence: Based on laser speckle imaging during hyperventilation shown in Figure 6F and consistent with previous findings (Boedtkjer et al., 2016c).

claim: When whisker stimulation was performed during hyperventilation, there was an even more prominent difference in cerebral perfusion between WT and RPTPγ KO mice.
source: When whisker stimulation was performed during hyperventilation, we saw an even more prominent difference in cerebral perfusion between WT and RPTPγ KO mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: Based on laser speckle imaging during combined hyperventilation and whisker stimulation shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The 72 carriers of predicted loss-of-function PTPRG variants with moderate or high impact showed substantially elevated risk of a combined vascular disease phenotype encompassing cerebral infarct, angina pectoris, acute myocardial infarction, and acute vascular disorders of the intestine.
source: The 72 carriers of predicted loss-of-function PTPRG variants with moderate or high impact showed substantially elevated risk (Figure 7A) of a combined vascular disease phenotype encompassing the three vascular beds functionally investigated in this study (Figures 2–6): cerebral infarct (ICD-10 diagnosis code I63), angina pectoris (ICD-10 diagnosis code I20), acute myocardial infarction (ICD-10 diagnosis code I21), and acute vascular disorders of the intestine (ICD-10 diagnosis code K55.0).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of UK Biobank data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The 123 carriers of predicted loss-of-function PTPRG variants with low impact had a risk similar to non-carriers for the aggregated phenotype of acute vascular disease.
source: In contrast, the 123 carriers of predicted loss-of-function PTPRG variants with low impact as well as the 29,975 carriers of one or more missense PTPRG variants had a risk similar to non-carriers for this aggregated phenotype of acute vascular disease (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of UK Biobank data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The 29,975 carriers of one or more missense PTPRG variants had a risk similar to non-carriers for the aggregated phenotype of acute vascular disease.

evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of UK Biobank data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Carriers of moderate- and high-impact loss-of-function PTPRG variants had dramatically increased risk (~7 fold) of cerebral infarction.
source: The carriers of these most severe loss-of-function variants had dramatically increased risk (~7 fold) of cerebral infarction whereas the risk of acute myocardial infarction showed a tendency toward elevation that did not reach statistical significance (Figure 7B).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of UK Biobank data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The risk of acute myocardial infarction in carriers of moderate- and high-impact loss-of-function PTPRG variants showed a tendency toward elevation that did not reach statistical significance.
source: The carriers of these most severe loss-of-function variants had dramatically increased risk (~7 fold) of cerebral infarction whereas the risk of acute myocardial infarction showed a tendency toward elevation that did not reach statistical significance (Figure 7B).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of UK Biobank data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The risk of self-reported heart attacks was greatly elevated (~4 fold) amongst individuals carrying loss-of-function PTPRG variants of moderate and high impact.
source: To complement the evidence based on ICD-10 diagnosis codes, we further evaluated whether carriers of missense and loss-of-function variants in PTPRG differed in self-reported diseases compared to non-carriers (Figure 7C). The risk of self-reported heart attacks was greatly elevated (~4 fold) amongst individuals carrying loss-of-function PTPRG variants of moderate and high impact (Figure 7C).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of UK Biobank self-reported data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The risk of self-reported stroke showed a strong tendency toward elevation—with borderline statistical significance—amongst the carriers of moderate- and high-impact loss-of-function PTPRG variants.
source: The risk of self-reported stroke also showed a strong tendency toward elevation—with borderline statistical significance—amongst the carriers of moderate- and high-impact loss-of-function PTPRG variants (Figure 7C).
evidence: Based on logistic regression analysis of UK Biobank self-reported data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Carriers of high-impact loss-of-function PTPRG variants had a significantly lower left ventricular ejection fraction compared to non-carriers.
source: As cardiac pumping function often deteriorates following coronary ischemia, we next evaluated the cardiac contractile function in PTPRG loss-of-function carriers amongst the 12,851 exome-sequenced UK Biobank participants with available cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. We observed a significantly lower left ventricular ejection fraction in carriers of high-impact loss-of-function PTPRG variants compared to non-carriers (Figure 7D) consistent with the greater risk of ischemic heart disease (Figure 7C).
evidence: Based on multiple linear regression analysis of UK Biobank cardiac MRI data shown in Figure 7D.

evidence: Summary statement based on multiple experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inadequate tissue perfusion relative to metabolic demand is a fundamental pathophysiological cause of acute cardiovascular disease such as myocardial infarction and stroke.
source: Inadequate tissue perfusion relative to metabolic demand is a fundamental pathophysiological cause of acute (e.g. myocardial infarction and stroke) and chronic (e.g. heart failure and neurodegenerative disorders) cardiovascular disease.
evidence: Statement based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Inadequate tissue perfusion relative to metabolic demand is a fundamental pathophysiological cause of chronic cardiovascular disease such as heart failure and neurodegenerative disorders.

evidence: Statement based on established medical knowledge.

claim: The cellular and molecular mechanisms responsible for sensing metabolic disturbances and responding to inadequate perfusion are not well understood.
source: Despite their obvious clinical importance, the cellular and molecular mechanisms responsible for sensing metabolic disturbances and responding to inadequate perfusion are not well understood (Boedtkjer, 2018).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Boedtkjer, 2018.

claim: Local acidification is an important signal of insufficient nutrient delivery and waste product elimination.
source: Local acidification is an important signal of insufficient nutrient delivery and waste product elimination.
evidence: Statement based on established physiological knowledge.

claim: Functional effects of H+ in the vascular wall have long been appreciated.
source: Although functional effects of H+ in the vascular wall have long been appreciated (Boedtkjer, 2018; Gaskell, 1880; Boedtkjer et al., 2016a; Boedtkjer and Aalkjaer, 2012; Boedtkjer and Aalkjaer, 2013a; Boedtkjer and Aalkjaer, 2013b), the consequences of associated changes in CO2/HCO3– buffer composition have received far less attention.
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations including historical reference to Gaskell, 1880.

claim: The consequences of changes in CO2/HCO3– buffer composition have received far less attention than the effects of H+.

evidence: Statement based on review of literature.

claim: CO2 and HCO3– constitute an important buffer pair that minimizes acute changes in pH.
source: CO2 and HCO3– constitute an important buffer pair that minimizes acute changes in pH (Roos and Boron, 1981), improves spatial H+ mobility (Spitzer et al., 2002; Boedtkjer et al., 2016b), and provides substrate for acid-base transporters in cell membranes (Aalkjaer and Hughes, 1991; Boedtkjer et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Roos and Boron, 1981.

claim: CO2 and HCO3– improve spatial H+ mobility.
source: CO2 and HCO3– constitute an important buffer pair that minimizes acute changes in pH (Roos and Boron, 1981), improves spatial H+ mobility (Spitzer et al., 2002; Boedtkjer et al., 2016b), and provides substrate for acid-base transporters in cell membranes (Aalkjaer and Hughes, 1991; Boedtkjer et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to Spitzer et al., 2002 and Boedtkjer et al., 2016b.

claim: CO2 and HCO3– provide substrate for acid-base transporters in cell membranes.

evidence: Statement supported by citations to Aalkjaer and Hughes, 1991 and Boedtkjer et al., 2006.

claim: Evidence supports that cells possess sensors that respond to changes in [HCO3–] in the intracellular and extracellular space.

evidence: Statement supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2016, Boedtkjer et al., 2016c, and Chen et al., 2000.

claim: Through mechanisms that require RPTPγ, isolated decreases in extracellular [HCO3–] enhance HCO3– reabsorption in the renal proximal tubule when pCO2 and pH are kept constant.
source: Through mechanisms that require the transmembrane Receptor Protein Tyrosine Phosphatase (RPTP)γ, isolated decreases in extracellular [HCO3–] enhance HCO3– reabsorption in the renal proximal tubule (Zhou et al., 2016) and contractions of basilar arteries (Boedtkjer et al., 2016c) when pCO2 and pH are kept constant using out-of-equilibrium technology (Zhao et al., 1995).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: Through mechanisms that require RPTPγ, isolated decreases in extracellular [HCO3–] enhance contractions of basilar arteries when pCO2 and pH are kept constant.

evidence: Statement supported by citation to Boedtkjer et al., 2016c.

claim: The extracellular domain of RPTPγ resembles the active site of the carbonic anhydrases.
source: The extracellular domain of RPTPγ resembles the active site of the carbonic anhydrases (Barnea et al., 1993) and therefore likely binds HCO3–.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Barnea et al., 1993.

claim: HCO3– may induce a dimerization-dependent auto-inhibitory response in RPTPγ and thereby regulate signaling via the intracellular tyrosine phosphatase domains.

claim: CO2 has no direct net effect on cerebrovascular tone.
source: Although CO2 has no direct net effect on cerebrovascular tone (Boedtkjer et al., 2016c), respiratory changes leading to hyper- or hypocapnia will lead to secondary rises or falls in [HCO3–] and pH that in turn influence artery contractions and tissue perfusion.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Boedtkjer et al., 2016c.

claim: Predicted loss-of-function variants in PTPRG are associated with human ischemic vascular disease in the heart and brain.
source: Through translational genetic studies in the UK Biobank cohort (Bycroft et al., 2018), we further substantiate the importance of the identified mechanisms for human cardiovascular health as we demonstrate that predicted loss-of-function variants in PTPRG, encoding RPTPγ, are associated with human ischemic vascular disease in the heart and brain.
evidence: Based on genetic association studies in UK Biobank cohort.

claim: PTPRG is an ischemia susceptibility locus.
source: We conclude that PTPRG is an ischemia susceptibility locus; and RPTPγ-dependent sensing of HCO3– adjusts endothelium-mediated vasorelaxation, microvascular perfusion, and blood pressure during acid-base disturbances and altered tissue metabolism.
evidence: Conclusion based on genetic association studies and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reduced endothelial intracellular Ca2+ responses in arteries from RPTPγ KO mice in presence of CO2/HCO3– likely explain the observed mixed attenuation of NO-mediated and EDH-type vasorelaxation.
source: Reduced endothelial intracellular Ca2+ responses in arteries from RPTPγ KO mice in presence of CO2/HCO3– likely explain the observed mixed attenuation of NO-mediated and EDH-type vasorelaxation (Figures 2 and 3) as these responses rely on the Ca2+-sensitive NO-synthase and on intermediate- (IKCa) and small-conductance (SKCa) Ca2+-activated K+-channels, respectively (Figure 5O).
evidence: Inference based on Ca2+ imaging data and vasorelaxation experiments, considering known Ca2+-sensitivity of NO-synthase and Ca2+-activated K+-channels.

claim: NO-mediated and EDH-type vasorelaxation rely on the Ca2+-sensitive NO-synthase and on intermediate- (IKCa) and small-conductance (SKCa) Ca2+-activated K+-channels, respectively.

claim: A recent meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies linked PTPRG to ischemic stroke in African Americans.

evidence: Statement supported by citation to Carty et al., 2015.

claim: Using out-of-equilibrium technology, RPTPγ responds to changes in extracellular [HCO3–] independently of pCO2 and pH.

evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous work (Boedtkjer et al., 2016c).

claim: In cerebral resistance arteries, HCO3– contributes to buffering of acute acid loads.
source: The current study adds to our growing appreciation that acid-base equivalents, and HCO3– in particular, fulfill multifaceted functions (Boedtkjer et al., 2016a). In cerebral resistance arteries, HCO3– (a) contributes to buffering of acute acid loads (Rasmussen and Boedtkjer, 2018), (b) serves as substrate particularly for the Na+,HCO3–-cotransporter NBCn1 that protects against intracellular acidification (Thomsen et al., 2014), and (c) is sensed by RPTPγ to regulate cerebral perfusion (Figure 6).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Rasmussen and Boedtkjer, 2018.

claim: In cerebral resistance arteries, HCO3– serves as substrate particularly for the Na+,HCO3–-cotransporter NBCn1 that protects against intracellular acidification.

evidence: Statement supported by citation to Thomsen et al., 2014.

evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

evidence: Statement supported by citations to Boedtkjer et al., 2011, Boedtkjer et al., 2012, and Thomsen et al., 2014.

claim: Acting as a brake on vasodilation in regions of unmet metabolic demand, RPTPγ could reduce the degree of edema and consequent tissue damage caused by unopposed H+-induced vasodilation.

claim: Ptprg mRNA is found in arteriolar, capillary, as well as venular endothelial cells.
source: As illustrated in Figure 1D and E, Ptprg mRNA is found in arteriolar, capillary, as well as venular endothelial cells (Kalucka et al., 2020; Vanlandewijck et al., 2018), and it remains a future task to evaluate physiological and pathophysiological roles of RPTPγ in these individual blood vessel segments.
evidence: Based on single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1D,E and supported by citations to Kalucka et al., 2020 and Vanlandewijck et al., 2018.

claim: Transcript levels for Ptprg appear particularly high in a smaller subset of endothelial cells (up to 20–40%, depending on the vascular bed).

evidence: Based on single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: A distinct population of endothelial cells may act as the primary sensors of the metabolic environment.

evidence: Speculative inference based on the observation of heterogeneous Ptprg expression in endothelial cells.
